source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: Riddles built to need restructuring (constraint relaxation, chunk decomposition) are far harder for 38 LLMs than for people in a zero-shot, no-retrieval test.
numbers: 201 riddles; 120-item human subset (n=126 people, mean 52.9%). Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6% on subset. Full 201: 9.42% vs 19.25%, pooled odds ratio 2.29. GPT-5 inside human 95% CI. Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date did.
limits: No model-by-model significance tests vs humans; wordplay in Japanese may favour human childhood familiarity; auto-scored by gold-answer variants.
agent_relevance: Plain scaling and plain reasoning mode do not fix restructuring; need an explicit step that forces a new representation.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark) - verification failure
finding: Models often write the correct answer inside their reasoning and then do not commit to it. Generation works better than endorsement.
numbers: Verification failures = 5.23% (Gemini 2.5 Flash prev.) to 39.34% (Grok 4) of incorrect answers; Claude Opus 4 25.00%; DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57%. Counted when a gold variant appears in the thought log before the final answer.
limits: Literal string match, so it can over- or under-count; only 4 models had usable thought logs.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side check that accepts a candidate which passes the stated checks and stops (G2/G3 style), instead of letting the model keep exploring.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark) - language of thought
finding: Reasoning in Japanese vs English gave inconsistent effects on accuracy, so surface language is not the bottleneck.
numbers: Grok-4: Japanese 29.5% (33/112) vs English 48.8% (40/82), Fisher p=0.0071; Claude Opus 4: 36.7% vs 28.7%, p=0.356; Gemini 2.5 Flash: 0/12 vs 22/188, p=0.369; DeepSeek-R1 100% Japanese, 23.1%.
limits: Language choice not randomised; model picks it per item.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a translate/restate step alone to deliver a representation change.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Best LLM (ChatGPT) sits halfway between chance and people on puzzles that punish default commonsense; the errors are memorisation and commonsense association.
numbers: Humans 91.98% (sentence) and 91.67% (word) on 102 sampled items by 3 experts. ChatGPT overall 62.68% sentence, 53.46% word; random about 25%. Most other models near random. Few-shot and commonsense-augmented models gave limited gains.
quote: models' lateral thinking is often hindered by memorization and misleading commonsense associations
limits: Multiple choice; ChatGPT (2023) is old; some puzzles are probably in training data.
agent_relevance: Common-sense default is the fixated representation; an O4-style step that asks which default assumption the answer relies on targets this exact failure.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER - consistency
finding: When the same puzzle is reworded (semantic) or moved to a new story (context), people hold steady and models collapse, which says models matched surface form and did not restructure.
numbers: Humans: minimal drop on group-based accuracy (about 89-91%). ChatGPT failed 45% of original/semantic puzzles it got right in the context version (RoBERTa-L 61%). Group-based scores for models fall well below instance-based ones (for example single digits to low 20s for several models).
limits: Table was garbled in text extraction; exact cell-to-model mapping partly unclear, so only the headline gaps are used.
agent_relevance: Use mutation/rewording as the held-out test (G3) when judging whether a reframing really worked.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) SemEval-2024 Task 9: BRAINTEASER
finding: A shared task with 182 teams and 483 submissions: top systems reached near-ceiling on the 120-item test, but consistency drops on reconstructions remained.
numbers: Top word-puzzle team 0.983 overall, HW-TSC 0.967, Maxine 0.958; baselines human 0.920/0.917, ChatGPT 0.627/0.535, RoBERTa-L 0.434/0.207. 60% of participants fine-tuned, 65% prompted. Few-shot prompting helped consistency on word puzzles but not sentence puzzles.
quote: The best-performing systems reach 100% on both tasks, making it seem that the task is solved
limits: Test set only 120 items per subtask; fine-tuned systems learn recurring lateral patterns (shortcut learning); authors say the task is not solved.
agent_relevance: High scores come from fine-tuning on the pattern or tuned prompts; a scaffold with no training must lean on checks, not recognition.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall (OCW)
finding: Removing deliberate misleading groups (red herrings) makes LLM grouping far easier, which fits a fixation or Einstellung reading.
numbers: 618 walls; test 494. GPT-4 0-shot: OCW 6 solved walls/239 correct groups; OCW-Randomized (red herrings diluted) 59/595; OCW-WordNet (none) 471/1926. GPT-3.5 0-shot 0/114 -> 5/274 -> 337/1522. Humans 285/494 walls, 1405/1976 groups. More in-context examples (1 to 10 shot) did not help.
quote: red herrings... impede human performance in such tasks via the fixation effect and Einstellung paradigm
limits: Randomized and WordNet sets also change the knowledge needed, so the effect is not purely red-herring; no human test of the synthetic sets.
agent_relevance: A first-plausible grouping is the trap; scaffold should force alternatives that explain leftover items before commit.

source: Samadarshi et al. (2024) Connecting the Dots: NYT Connections
finding: On 438 NYT Connections games, the best LLM solves few games fully; red-herring words and categories cause most mistakes; experts beat it clearly.
numbers: Best model Claude 3.5 Sonnet fully solves 18% of games; experts perfectly solved over 60% of games; novices only a little above the model. Few-shot and chain-of-thought used.
limits: Single-attempt format (all four groups at once) differs from the real game, which gives feedback after each group.
agent_relevance: The real game gives feedback per group; our loop with a checker mirrors that easier, feedback form.

source: NYT-Connections benchmark (2024) A Deceptively Simple Text Classification Task that Stumps System-1 Thinkers
finding: Chain-of-thought and self-consistency give diminishing returns as red-herring difficulty rises; a trivial similarity heuristic matches some LLMs.
numbers: Best model (Claude 3.5) 40.25% vs humans 60.67% with full hints; with no hints Claude 11% vs humans 39.33%. Simple heuristic 13.25% (no hints). LLaMA 3 70B 23.75% no hints, 28.5% with hints. Gap to humans about 30 points.
quote: CoT and Self-Consistency show diminishing returns as task difficulty increases
limits: Dataset small; hints change the task; models are 2024 vintage.
agent_relevance: More sampled chains do not break a wrong frame; the frame must be changed, not re-sampled.

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks: Visual Symbolic Compositional Reasoning with Matchstick Puzzles
finding: First large LLM test on Knoblich-style matchstick arithmetic (move one or two sticks). Models fail mostly where the operator must change, the constraint people find hardest to drop.
numbers: 1.4M generated puzzles; 400-item test; 14 vision-language models. With text: o3 60.00%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 45.25%, Gemini-2.5-Flash 26.50%, GPT-4o 0.00%. Without text o3 38.50% (average across regimes 49.25%). Humans 91.72%. 4.18% of generated items one-stick, 82.01% two-stick.
quote: models are biased toward digit-level manipulations rather than considering operator edits
limits: Not Roman numerals and not the original Knoblich type labels; tests perception plus search; human sample small.
agent_relevance: Operator change is the failing slot; scaffold O4 should name operator and type constraints explicitly, not only digit edits.

source: Ji et al. (2025) MathSticks - fine-grained breakdown
finding: Accuracy falls when the equation needs a sign change and when several solutions exist; digit edits are favoured.
numbers: Authors' prose: two-stick puzzles harder than one-stick; multiple-solution items 20-30 points harder for o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro; Gemini-2.5-Pro one-move 51.7% with text vs 25.8% pure visual. Table 4 (text prompt) shows sign-changed lower than no-sign-change for every model (for example 23.94% vs 29.20%; row alignment in the extraction is uncertain).
limits: Row alignment in the extracted table is uncertain; authors' prose is the safer source for direction.
agent_relevance: Chunk decomposition in digit shapes is handled better than operator relaxation; prompts should enumerate constraint types (value, operator, tautology).

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Mid-trace Aha shifts in RL-trained reasoning models are rare and usually do not help accuracy.
numbers: 1M+ traces, 3 domains (crosswords, math, Rush Hour), Qwen2.5 and Llama GRPO runs, 4 temperatures. Shifts in 6.31% of traces overall; accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for non-shifted traces. DeepSeek-R1 shifts 0.00-0.25%, GPT-4o 0.88-2.21%. Formal detector fires on 1.79% of samples.
quote: reasoning shifts are rare, do not become more frequent with training, and seldom improve accuracy
limits: Shift is defined by a trace rubric; small trained models; original R1-Zero claim not retested at full scale.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous 'wait' restructuring is not a dependable mechanism; do not count on it, trigger it by signal (G1).

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) Illusion of Insight - forced reconsideration
finding: A cue that forces a second pass ('Wait, we need to reconsider') raises accuracy mainly on math, and most when the first pass was high-entropy.
numbers: Paired N: 83,200 crosswords, 320,000 math, 320,000 Rush Hour. Math 0.3221 -> 0.4062 (+8.41 pp; 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong). Crosswords 0.0970 -> 0.1015 (+0.45 pp; 5,380 vs 5,004). Rush Hour +0.01 pp (base rate 0.0002).
limits: Gain from a second sample versus the cue itself not separated in what I read; small models; no restructuring-specific tasks.
agent_relevance: Confirms uncertainty-gated reconsideration (G1 plus an entropy-like signal) has measurable value; effect is domain-specific and can be near zero.

source: Qiu, Zhou and Schooler (2026) The Cost of Coordination: Why Multi-Agent LLMs Explore More But Discover Less (CogSci 48)
finding: Framed in Ohlsson's theory, two-agent GPT-4o teams solve situation puzzles (restructuring) worse than a single agent although they ask more varied questions.
numbers: N=82 trials (30-min: 25 solo, 25 team; 1-hour: 16 solo, 16 team), 3 puzzles each, host Gemini-2.0-flash. Total questions per session solo 179.9 vs team 49.2 (30 min); 374.8 vs 95.9 (1 h). Team deficit: 47% via fewer host questions (indirect -0.370, CI [-0.560,-0.183]), 53% direct (beta=-0.415, p=.005). Team question diversity higher (beta=0.556, p<.001). Question warmness predicted found elements (beta=0.060, p<.001).
quote: teams were significantly less accurate than solo agents despite asking questions across broad categories
limits: Own puzzles, one model pair, unstructured teams; raw accuracy per condition not captured in the text I read.
agent_relevance: More voices or more breadth is not insight; G4 (no persona voters on single-answer problems) fits.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT scored at the most likely human level on 30 classic verbal insight problems, with feedback after each practice problem.
numbers: 15 practice + 15 transfer problems; ChatGPT correct on 7/15 practice and 5/15 transfer (12/30). Compared with per-problem solution rates of 20 human subjects; its answer pattern is within the top 5% most probable for humans on practice set.
limits: Single run, 2023 model, feedback given on practice set, no repeated sampling; items are famous so contamination is likely.
agent_relevance: Famous items hide the real gap; use fresh or perturbed problems.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: GPT models beat people on verbal insight problems but are worse on a representational change task built from rebus puzzles, and use reasoning where people use transformation.
numbers: Exp 6: humans more accurate than GPT-4-turbo (estimate 0.46, CI [0.41,0.51]) and GPT-4o (0.31, CI [0.25,0.36]), p<.001; 24 problems, 4 options each (correct RC, semantic-related, irrelevant, exclusion). Strategy in correct trials: GPT-4o reasoning 68.88%, GPT-4-turbo 71.26%; humans transformation 72.41%. 61 humans, 61 runs per model.
quote: strong performance in creative tasks is likely driven by non-creative mechanisms
limits: Multiple choice with image plus text; budget limits meant no repeated GPT sampling for some tasks (authors).
agent_relevance: Model success on insight sets may come from reasoning over the options; recognising a new representation among choices is the weak step.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Mental-set test (shortcut vs long method) on 6+6 equivalence problems: few-shot models fall back on the familiar method, and zero-shot chain-of-thought raises accuracy but at 3 steps instead of 1.
numbers: Exact match: GPT-4o few-shot shortcut 0.33 vs complex 0.66; Llama-3.1-8B 0.16 vs 0; with CoT GPT-4o 0.66 vs 0.83, Llama-70B 0.5 vs 0.66. Example order changed scores by up to 0.66 (Llama-70B complex, few-shot). Successful answers: 1 step (few-shot) vs 3 steps (few-shot+CoT).
limits: Only six problems per condition so scores move in steps of 0.16; no significance tests; read via an ar5iv summary page.
agent_relevance: Order of examples (shortcut first vs complex first) changes outcomes: the example set itself can set a mental set.

source: Solving Situation Puzzles with Large Language Model and External Reformulation (2025)
finding: A program that restarts the dialogue with the original story plus selected Yes/No answers (reformulation) raises win rate on situation puzzles; the model is not asked to restructure itself.
numbers: 5 puzzles, max 30 questions and 5 guesses; K=5 rounds, M=3 hints. Wins baseline 2/5 vs 4/5; questions 28.6 vs 22.6; guesses 2.8 vs 2.4; Yes-questions 3.6 vs 5; No-questions 18.2 vs 12.2. Ablation: K=10/M=6 and wrong-guess-only both 3/5 wins.
limits: Five puzzles, no variance or significance test; one run per puzzle; model identity not captured.
agent_relevance: A working analog of O6 in an agent loop: code compresses what was learned and starts a fresh frame at set points. Test with proper n.

source: Williamson et al. (2025) Syntactic Blind Spots: How Misalignment Leads to LLMs' Mathematical Errors
finding: Rewording a wrongly answered math question to a simpler structure recovers many answers, so some errors are a surface-form to strategy mismatch.
numbers: Improvement up to 15.5 percentage points (Granite on MultiArith); recovered answers range 2 (Qwen, MultiArith) to 210 (Gemma, ASDiv); gains larger on GSM8K and SVAMP. Higher dependency-locality score goes with higher failure rate.
limits: Rephrased only the items the model got wrong, so regression to the mean and resampling luck are not ruled out (no resample control found in the text I read).
agent_relevance: Cheap O6 test: restate the failing item in a simpler frame and compare against a plain resample at equal tokens.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) RM-PoT: Reformulating Mathematical Problems and Solving via Program of Thoughts
finding: Rewriting the problem into several surface forms before solving is a reformulation step; authors report surface-form changes alter the answer distribution and solve rate.
numbers: Method: reformulate, retrieve 5 domain examples, run Python code. Exact benchmark gains not captured in my read.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read in detail; no benchmark numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Same family as O6; check numbers before use.

source: Voboril and Szeider (2026) Improving Constraint Models with LLM Agents
finding: An agent that proposes a different constraint model and checks it against the original improves 68.5% of cases, but best-of-k does about as well.
numbers: 15 combinatorial problems, 10 runs each, 10 test instances: better in 1028 of 1500 (68.5%), mean relative objective change +14.7%. Out of 150: single-shot 64, best-of-5 101, ReAct agent mean 102.8.
limits: Agent adds little over equal-budget sampling with the same validator; optimisation domain, not human insight tasks.
agent_relevance: Honest control: a validator plus samples may give most of the benefit of a restructuring agent.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Learn to Relax with LLMs: AutoCO (ACL 2026)
finding: An LLM proposes which constraints to relax, with MCTS over relaxation paths plus evolutionary search; used in constraint optimisation, an explicit machine version of constraint relaxation.
numbers: 24.7% average optimality-gap reduction vs state-of-the-art LLM methods on three benchmarks; VRPTW-fuel gaps 0.31 (S) and 0.00 (M) vs ReEvo 0.36 and 0.20; ablations cost 14.10 to 23.73% performance.
limits: Optimisation benchmarks; no human-insight comparison.
agent_relevance: Shows relaxing a named constraint inside a solver loop works; O4 needs the list of constraints and a checker.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider and Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Human baseline for every machine paper: matchstick arithmetic difficulty follows the constraints to be relaxed and the tightness of chunks.
numbers: Exp 1A: fewer Type B than Type A solved (p<.05), fewer Type C than Type B (p<.01), fewer Type D (tight chunk) than Type A (p<.05); solution times A faster than B (N=20, T=12, p<.001), B faster than C (T=41, p<.05), A faster than D (T=10, p<.001).
limits: Human data; only matchstick Roman numerals; machine studies above use different items so no direct match.
agent_relevance: Defines the constraint types (value, operator, tautology) our O4 prompt can enumerate.

source: Nasvytis and Fan (2026) Leveraging Speech to Identify Signatures of Insight and Transfer in Problem Solving
finding: Human think-aloud on matchstick arithmetic: participants who saw the same solution type improved fastest and began to name the problem type.
numbers: N=189; five problems; Same condition success rose from 0.32 (trial 1) to 0.75 (trial 5).
limits: Human study, no model; only abstract and first pages read.
agent_relevance: Naming the problem type may mark a transferable restructure: log the named constraint for reuse.

source: Oellinger, Jones and Knoblich (2006) Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick arithmetic tasks
finding: Abstract-level only: representational change dominates solution rate; heuristics matter little; the model makes representational change the condition for applying heuristics.
numbers: 120 solvers on two kinds of two-move tasks (from abstract).
limits: Not opened (full-text download failed); model internals unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Candidate older computational account to read next.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight
finding: Abstract-level: tests representational change against progress monitoring on an unlimited-move task with eye tracking; not read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; I could not confirm a running computational model.
agent_relevance: Pointer only; do not cite numbers.

source: Frontiers in Psychology (2025) interactive matchstick algebra, movement and constraint relaxation
finding: Search snippet only: interactive solving helps matchstick algebra, but movement mainly interferes with constraint relaxation rather than aiding chunk decomposition.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Search summary only.
